results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 52 outline summaries match the controlling ideas of their aligned spec paragraphs, in spec order.
Same as the reverse-outline result: same controlling ideas, same order.
Introduction ¶4: the outliner's two ideas are the two halves of the thesis statement, which the spec (p04) places in one unit as one claim.
In Practice ¶9: announced as 'Two details deserve a sentence', the paragraph's single job is to explain two details of the worked table, as spec p45 declares.
Every unit supports one of S1-S5 or frames the chapter.

results.quote: Treat the percentages as history; keep the last finding.
results.finding: The adoption percentages (27%, 47%, one in ten) are given but not tied to the ownership decision the paragraph opens with; the reader is told to 'keep the last finding' without being told what it shows about whose sale it is.

The other tables (store additions, fiscal rules, components, services, requirements, choices, stages, worked example), figures and quotations are each introduced or followed by prose that says what they show.

results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva's jacket from Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand, travels from the Duiven warehouse to her Nijmegen door
results.finding: Declared contrast carrying over 'one channel acting on another channel's stock or order'; the paragraph opens with a signpost and a new case and never links back to that idea, so the boundary reads as a second opening rather than a contrast.

results.quote: **Whose sale is it.** Before a store ships its first web order, the merchant must decide whose sale it is
results.finding: Declared example relationship carrying over the stages and Kestrel & Pine's position into 'the joins in practice, starting with the ownership question'; the section opens on a bold lead with no sentence connecting it to the stages or presenting what follows as the joins in practice.

results.quote: **Ship-from-store on someone else's marketplace: Zalando Connected Retail, 2021 to 2027.** One marketplace program shows ship-from-store at scale.
results.finding: Declared as an example of the ownership question to settle before a store ships a web order; the Zalando paragraph is framed only as ship-from-store at scale and never refers to that question, so the declared relationship is not expressed (and may not fit the paragraph's content).

results.draft_locus: In Practice ¶9 -> When It Goes Wrong ¶1
results.quote: Stores fail in ways online systems do not, because people and buildings are involved.
results.finding: Declared contrast with the Utrecht pilot working with a buffer and a confirmation; the opening sentence contrasts stores with online systems instead and does not carry over the working pilot.
All other transition_in relationships are expressed at their boundaries.

results.quote: Before a store ships its first web order, the merchant must decide whose sale it is, and the old adoption figures show how often that was left open.
results.finding: Both flow readers report that the 'Whose sale is it' paragraph never says what the decision involves; its figures are mostly about adoption, so heading and content do not match and the 'keep the last finding' instruction is unclear.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 ("Before a store ships its first web order... The paragraph never explains what the decision involves")

results.quote: **Store orders in one order model.** A common order model can carry both store and web sales into finance
results.finding: Both flow readers mark the order of the items inside In Practice as unclear: a set of loosely connected bold-lead topics (whose sale, Zalando, order model, routing, PCI, worked example) with nothing saying why they come in this order.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 (In Practice: "Why these items come in this order is unclear")

results.quote: That is the ladder: simple rules in the platform, then an explainable routing decision separate from the deduction of stock, which is the OMS's job
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read this sentence: the 'ladder' arrives with no set-up and 'which' can refer to the routing decision or to the deduction of stock.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 ("That is the ladder... 'which' could refer to routing or to deduction")

results.quote: | | December 2026 (the Mirage) | Interim fix, from April 2027 | Target, from Q4 2027 |

results.quote: The classic field study found about two-thirds of store inventory records wrong
results.finding: The intro reader predicted the sections and their order correctly, but described the evidence as 'mostly a running fictional case' plus one field study; the expected vendor documentation and country fiscal rules as evidence are not predicted, because nothing in the introduction announces them. The spec's roadmap (p05) does not ask for the kinds of evidence either, so the criterion asks for something no introduction unit carries.
Reader names the up-to-a-day-old copy, the promise treated as commitment, the two-unit threshold, the staff confirmation with 'we confirm within two hours', and later POS stock events; no new POS.

Reader names the German fiscal check first (TSE, sequential numbers, registration) as able to rule a product out, then countries and store weight decide platform POS versus specialist POS by events through the order hub.
